input.question: What does the experimental and clinical literature actually show about self-touch / self-generated touch and sensory attenuation in patients with unilateral brain lesions — specifically: (1) whether the force-matching / sensory-attenuation paradigm has been tested in stroke patients with hemiplegia or hemisensory loss, (2) findings in right-hemisphere patients with hemispatial or personal neglect, anosognosia, somatoparaphrenia regarding self-touch, self-other attribution, or the ability to localise a body part touched by the intact hand, (3) evidence that self-touch (touching the affected limb with the intact hand) improves position sense, limb localisation, or body ownership in hemiplegic patients, and (4) any evidence on the crossed-finger / Aristotle illusion, the "self-touch" temporal-binding paradigm, or body-size/extent estimation in unilateral lesion patients.
input.context: Preparing a lesson on self-touch: components (motor command/efference copy, tactile reafference, proprioception), their integration for perceiving the spatial extent of the body, and the clinical outcomes in patients with unilateral lesions. I need accurate, citable findings for the clinical part — including null results and contested claims.

result.brief:
## Summary

Self-touch has been studied in unilateral-lesion patients, but the evidence is thin, unevenly distributed across the four sub-questions, and dominated by single-case reports. The best-replicated clinical finding is **self-touch enhancement of tactile *detection*** in stroke patients with primary sensory loss (first reported by Weiskrantz & Zhang; 22/39 patients in a later series, mostly right-hemisphere). By contrast, the force-matching/sensory-attenuation paradigm itself appears **never to have been applied to hemiplegic or hemisensory stroke patients**, self-touch has **not** been shown to improve position sense, the Aristotle/crossed-finger illusion has **no** published unilateral-lesion study, and the one adequately powered test of self-touch on limb ownership in right-hemisphere stroke found the benefit came from *experimenter*-administered touch, not self-touch.

## Findings

**Facet 1 — force-matching / sensory attenuation in stroke**

1. **The canonical paradigm is self-generated vs. externally-generated force.** Shergill, Bays, Frith & Wolpert showed that people perceive a force produced by their own other hand as weaker than an identical externally applied force, so they over-compensate and force escalates ("two eyes for an eye"). This is the reference paradigm your lesson's "motor command/efference copy" component rests on. [Shergill et al. 2003, *Science* 301:187](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12855800/)

2. **This paradigm does not appear to have been tested in hemiplegic or hemisensory-loss stroke.** Systematic querying of Europe PMC (queries combining "sensory attenuation"/"self-generated force"/"force matching" with stroke, hemiplegia, hemiparesis, parietal lesion) returned 100+ hits but none applying the self-vs-other attenuation contrast to a stroke sample. The sensory-attenuation patient literature is concentrated in schizophrenia/psychosis, functional neurological disorder, tics, ADHD and eating disorders — not focal lesions. [e.g. Rossi et al. 2025, scoping review of sensory attenuation in symptomatic and healthy individuals](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40625349/)

3. **What *has* been done in stroke is force-matching as a motor/precision task, not as an attenuation index.** Hemispheric stroke survivors show impaired joint-torque matching attributable to proprioceptive deficit — a statement about kinaesthetic acuity, not about attenuation of self-generated signals. [Oh, Rymer & Oh 2026, *Biomed Eng Lett*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42080035/) Similarly, force-matching in subacute stroke has been used to index muscle activation/co-activation rather than sensory attenuation. [Chow & Stokic 2021, *Exp Brain Res*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34213633/)

4. **The closest lesion analogue is a dissociation result, not an attenuation result.** In 20 left-hemisphere stroke patients, apraxic patients had a *prolonged* time window for sensorimotor integration (delay-detection threshold) but *preserved* explicit sense of agency — i.e., altered low-level prediction/feedback comparison with intact explicit self-attribution. [Nobusako et al. 2025, *Front Hum Neurosci*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12202472/)

5. **The neural substrate of attenuation is cerebellar–somatosensory, established only in healthy participants.** Attenuation of self-generated touch tracks cerebellum–somatosensory functional connectivity, and brief temporal perturbations of somatosensory reafference abolish both perceptual and neural attenuation while increasing SMA–cerebellar coupling. [Kilteni & Ehrsson 2020, *J Neurosci*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31811029/); [Kilteni, Houborg & Ehrsson 2023, *J Neurosci*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37339879/) This gives you a mechanistic scaffold, but it is not lesion evidence.

**Facet 2 — right-hemisphere patients: neglect, anosognosia, somatoparaphrenia, self–other attribution**

6. **"Touching the affected limb with the intact hand" is literally the diagnostic task for personal neglect — and RHD patients fail it.** Personal neglect is operationalised as failure to explore/touch one's own contralesional body with the intact hand (e.g., the Fluff test: patients must detach stickers from their own body). [Caggiano & Jehkonen 2018, *Neuropsychol Rev*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30547412/); [Cocchini & Beschin 2022, *Neuropsychol Rehabil*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723030/) This is the cleanest "self-touch as a clinical probe" finding in the literature.

7. **Key negative result: in right-hemisphere stroke, *other*-administered touch — not self-touch — increased limb ownership.** In 26 right-hemisphere patients, a significant increase in limb ownership followed **experimenter-administered** C-tactile-optimal (3 cm/s) touch; the self-generated condition did not produce the effect. Voxel-based lesion-symptom mapping associated failure to benefit with right insula and, more substantially, right **corpus callosum** damage. [Jenkinson et al. 2020, *Brain Commun*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7425337/) This is the strongest controlled evidence and it cuts against a simple "self-touch restores ownership" story.

8. **Single-case evidence does support self-touch in somatoparaphrenia — with an explicit/implicit dissociation.** In one somatoparaphrenic patient, self-administered touch increased *explicit* recognition of the disowned left hand, while implicitly both the patient's hand and the experimenter's hand were rated as more belonging — i.e., explicit and implicit ownership recovered differently. [Salvato, Crivelli, Gandola & Bottini 2023, *Neurocase* 29:133–140](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38650434/)

9. **The classic case (GE) shows self-touch reinstating ownership and affect — but also shows the effect is not limb-specific.** A patient with left hemiplegia, hemianaesthesia, neglect and anosognosia who spontaneously stroked her affected arm "with care and affection" regained ownership and positive affect when she touched her own arm; yet stroking four *foreign* arms (including a right rubber arm in an implausible position) also eventually produced ownership, and stroking a foreign arm transiently *disowned* her real arm until she touched it again. [van Stralen, van Zandvoort & Dijkerman 2011, *Phil Trans R Soc B* 366:3142–3152](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3172603/) Treat this as a demonstration of a general body-representation effect, not proof of a self-specific mechanism.

10. **Covert disownership is common and is missed by verbal interview.** In 105 stroke patients (55 controls), ~30% showed "covert disownership" of contralateral hand/arm/leg/face, revealed by non-verbal response; right insula and basal ganglia were implicated for upper-limb ownership, with large-scale bilateral temporo-parietal and fronto-occipital disconnections. [Cataldo E et al. 2025, *Brain Commun*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12204195/) This means incidence estimates based on interview alone understate the phenomenon.

11. **Anosognosia for hemiplegia has a partly separable substrate from somatoparaphrenia, and implicit knowledge is often preserved.** AHP occurs in ~18% of first-ever stroke and ~32% of right-hemisphere stroke patients, is associated with right insular damage, and patients show slowed processing of deficit-related sentences despite denying the deficit — implicit knowledge without explicit awareness. [van Stralen et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3172603/); for the lesion dissociations see [Moro et al. 2016, *Cortex*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27494375/) and the tripartite disconnection account in [Pacella et al. 2019, *eLife*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31383259/)

12. **Self-observation can restore motor awareness in AHP — a useful parallel for the "self-generated" theme.** Video self-observation improved motor awareness in anosognosic patients, indicating that re-presenting the patient's own action can partially correct the faulty comparison. [Besharati et al. 2015, *Neuropsychol Rehabil*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24958030/)

**Facet 3 — does self-touch improve detection, localisation, position sense, ownership?**

13. **Best-replicated clinical effect: self-touch enhances tactile *detection* in the affected hand.** First reported in a right-hemisphere stroke patient who could not detect examiner-administered touch but felt it when touched by her own unaffected hand or by a probe held in it; replicated in a larger series in which **22 of 39** stroke patients showed self-touch enhancement, **17 of 22** with right-hemisphere lesions. [Weiskrantz & Zhang; Valentini et al. — both reviewed in van Stralen et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3172603/)

14. **The mechanism appears to be temporal expectation, not proprioception or spatial attention.** When the affected hand was interdigitated with the examiner's so that proprioceptive input was uninformative, enhancement occurred only when the patient's *own* hand was touched; and introducing a temporal delay between the administering movement and the tactile stimulus **abolished** the enhancement. This is direct evidence against a proprioceptive explanation and for a prediction/timing account. [White et al., reviewed in van Stralen et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3172603/)

15. **The effect extends to the lower limb, using a self-touch rubber-hand proxy.** Patient NG, the first reported lower-limb case, could not reach her foot; using a prosthetic limb she administered stimulation herself while the examiner synchronously stimulated her affected left foot. She detected **all** self-administered stimulation but missed **one-third** of examiner-administered stimulation. [White & Aimola Davies 2013, *Perception* 42:473–476](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23866560/)

16. **Limb *localisation* improved under self-touch in one reported case — the single most on-point result for your question, but n=1.** A right-hemisphere stroke patient who could detect but not localise touch on the left hand improved localisation when reaching with the right hand to the left of the affected hand while experiencing an illusion of self-touch; the authors inferred that self-touch altered the representation of the affected hand. [White et al., reviewed in van Stralen et al. 2011](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3172603/)

17. **There is no evidence that self-touch improves *position sense* (proprioception) in hemiplegic patients.** No study measuring position sense as an outcome of self-touch was found; the review literature explicitly concludes proprioceptive information is *not* the primary contributor to the self-touch effect. What exists instead is body-*size* distortion (see 20–21) and general proprioceptive awareness work. Report this as a genuine null/gap rather than as a negative finding.

18. **In healthy participants, active self-touch causally restores proprioceptive spatial awareness when it has been experimentally disrupted** — the strongest causal support for the lesson's integration claim. Active self-touch restored bodily proprioceptive spatial awareness after disruption by the rubber hand illusion. [Cataldo, Crivelli, Bottini, Gomi & Haggard 2024, *Proc R Soc B*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38228504/)

19. **Bimanual self-touch depends on interhemispheric transfer — mechanistically linking self-touch to callosal integrity.** In a two-robot self-touch design, tactile events were transferred interhemispherically, but the *sign* of the tactile information was not respected (both increases and decreases in pressure enhanced the perceived bump), and randomising (rather than blocking) stimulus order abolished the effect — implying a stable model of temporally synchronised events is required. [Kong et al. 2022, *Proc R Soc B*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9727658/) Combined with finding 7 (right callosal damage predicting failure to benefit from touch), this is a strong, teachable bridge between mechanism and lesion.

**Facet 4 — Aristotle illusion, self-touch temporal binding, body-size/extent estimation**

20. **Body-size estimation in unilateral lesions points in *opposite* directions depending on the syndrome — a genuinely contested literature.** In 11 right-hemisphere hemiplegic patients, patients with personal neglect *underestimated* left-hand width, whereas hemiplegic patients *without* personal neglect tended to perceive the affected hand as **larger** than the ipsilesional one. [Caggiano et al. 2020, *J Clin Exp Neuropsychol*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33203298/)

21. **A larger study found transient *overestimation* of the paretic arm, which resolved.** In 32 right-hemisphere stroke patients (13 paresis alone, 10 paresis + neglect, 9 neither), measured by explicit visual, explicit tactile/proprioceptive, and implicit reaching estimates, the contralesional paretic arm was transiently **overestimated**; 19 patients re-examined ~5 months later showed resolution. [Shahvaroughi-Farahani et al. 2021, *PLoS One*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8177542/)

22. **Personal neglect produces a *labile*, not simply shrunken, body representation.** In 9 right-brain-damaged patients, PN+ patients showed a wider distorted representational range for both hands *and* face; PN− patients also misrepresented the left hand, linked to impaired motor performance. [Mora, Gonzalez Alted & Cocchini 2023, *Neuropsychologia*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36863608/) So the "downsized hand" and "enlarged paretic arm" findings coexist — present this as unresolved heterogeneity (small samples, different tasks, different syndromes).

23. **The self-touch paradigm has been used to show motor signals dominate perceived spatial extent — with a caveat.** Using two coupled master–slave robots to decouple motor from tactile extent, perceived *tactile* extent was strongly biased by movement amplitude, and touch also biased perceived *movement* extent; the movement→touch effect was stronger for active than passive movement, but motor dominance was **not total**. [Cataldo, Dupin, Gomi & Haggard 2021, *Neuropsychologia*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33346045/) This is the direct experimental basis for "integration for perceiving the spatial extent of the body" — but in healthy adults.

24. **Self-touch temporal binding is an active, contested research front — and the direction of the effect is disputed.** The bimanual self-touch paradigm shows that predictions of self-touch determine the temporal tuning of somatosensory perception, including temporal binding windows. [Cemeljic, Job & Kilteni 2025, *iScience*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39898028/); [Cemeljic & Kilteni 2026, *Eur J Neurosci*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41725123) Crucially, two recent papers reach **opposite conclusions**: "action does not enhance but attenuates predicted touch" [Job & Kilteni 2023, *eLife*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38099521/) versus "movement enhances tactile sensitivity through prediction" [D'Onofrio Pacheco & Zimmermann 2026, *J Neurophysiol*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41824129/). A divisive-normalisation account reconciles some of this by invoking noisy sensorimotor predictions. [Valè et al. 2025, *J Neurophysiol*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40531356/) Also note attenuation is not the same phenomenon as movement-related tactile gating. [Kilteni & Ehrsson 2022, *iScience*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35372807/)

25. **No published study tests the Aristotle (crossed-finger) illusion in unilateral-lesion patients.** Europe PMC returns only 14 items for "Aristotle illusion," none a stroke/lesion study: work exists in Parkinson's disease (where interdigit tactile perception was **normal**) [Fiorio et al. 2014, *PLoS One*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3921216/), in healthy somatotopic/directional-judgement paradigms [de Haan, Anema & Dijkerman 2012, *PLoS One*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3454417/), on hand posture and perceived tactile distance [Longo 2017, *Sci Rep*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28851889/), and fMRI decoding [Lee et al. 2025, *Front Neurosci*](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40613086/). If you want to teach crossed-finger effects in lesions, you must flag it as an untested extrapolation.

## Sources

**Kept**
- van Stralen, van Zandvoort & Dijkerman (2011), *Phil Trans R Soc B* — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3172603/ — the single most important source: a review *plus* primary case (GE) dedicated exactly to self-touch in post-stroke somatosensory and body-representation disorders. Source of findings 8, 11, 13, 14, 16.
- Jenkinson et al. (2020), *Brain Commun* — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7425337/ — the only adequately powered (n=26) self- vs other-generated touch test in right-hemisphere stroke; supplies the key null result and callosal VLSM.
- Cataldo E et al. (2025), *Brain Commun* — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12204195/ — large (n=105) modern incidence and lesion-network data on disownership.
- Salvato et al. (2023), *Neurocase* — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38650434/ — most recent self-touch-in-somatoparaphrenia case, with explicit/implicit dissociation.
- White & Aimola Davies (2013), *Perception* — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23866560/ — lower-limb self-touch enhancement; practical paradigm for mobility-limited patients.
- Shahvaroughi-Farahani et al. (2021), *PLoS One* — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8177542/ — best-controlled body-size data in paretic stroke, with follow-up.
- Caggiano et al. (2020) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33203298/; Mora et al. (2023) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36863608/ — the contradicting body-size results; essential for the "contested" framing.
- Cataldo A et al. (2021), *Neuropsychologia* — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33346045/; and (2024), *Proc R Soc B* — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38228504/ — the robot self-touch spatial-extent paradigm and the causal restoration result.
- Kong et al. (2022), *Proc R Soc B* — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9727658/ — interhemispheric transfer in bimanual self-touch; the mechanistic hinge for lesion interpretation.
- Cemeljic/Job/Kilteni (2025) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39898028/; Job & Kilteni (2023) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38099521/; D'Onofrio Pacheco & Zimmermann (2026) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41824129/; Valè et al. (2025) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40531356/ — the temporal-binding paradigm and its live contradiction.
- Shergill et al. (2003), *Science* — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12855800/ — the force-matching paradigm's origin; needed to state precisely what was *not* done in stroke.
- Oh, Rymer & Oh (2026) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42080035/ — documents that force matching in stroke indexes proprioceptive acuity, not attenuation.
- Nobusako et al. (2025), *Front Hum Neurosci* — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12202472/ — stroke lesion study of sensorimotor integration window vs explicit agency.
- Fiorio et al. (2014) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3921216/; de Haan et al. (2012) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3454417/ — establish the Aristotle-illusion literature base and its non-lesion scope.
- Pacella et al. (2019), *eLife* — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31383259/; Moro et al. (2016), *Cortex* — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27494375/; Besharati et al. (2015) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24958030/ — anosognosia substrate and self-observation effects.
- Caggiano & Jehkonen (2018) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30547412/; Cocchini & Beschin (2022) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32723030/ — personal neglect as a self-touch-to-own-body task; the Fluff test.
- Kilteni & Ehrsson (2020) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31811029/; Kilteni, Houborg & Ehrsson (2023) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37339879/ — cerebellar substrate of attenuation (healthy).

**Dropped**
- Large numbers of tangential Europe PMC hits (post-stroke fatigue, gait/biomechanics, robotic rehabilitation, neuroimaging methods, sensor technology, COVID/fatigue commentary) — retrieved because broad Boolean terms matched, but irrelevant to self-touch or attribution.
- Schizophrenia/psychosis, ADHD, autism, anorexia and dissociation self-touch papers — mechanistically informative but not lesion evidence; would dilute the clinical section. (Retained only the general scoping review as a scope statement.)
- Preprints duplicating published versions (e.g., the bioRxiv divisive-attenuation and Research Square anorexia preprints) — superseded by peer-reviewed versions.
- Paywalled items for which only abstracts were available and whose abstracts did not yield a distinct citable claim.

## Gaps

1. **Facet 1 is essentially unanswered in the literature, not by me.** No study applies the self-vs-external force-matching (or equivalent) attenuation contrast to hemiplegic/hemisensory stroke patients. I searched ~10 query formulations across Europe PMC; the absence is consistent across them. If a study exists, it is likely titled around "sense of effort," "force perception," or "agency" rather than "sensory attenuation" — worth a targeted search by author (e.g., the Sirigu/Lafargue sense-of-effort line, or Gandevia/McCloskey lineage) which I could not pursue without a working search engine.
2. **Position sense as an outcome of self-touch is untested** in hemiplegia. Anyone claiming self-touch improves position sense in stroke is extrapolating from healthy samples and from *detection*/localisation data.
3. **Aristotle/crossed-finger illusion in unilateral lesions: no published study.** Do not present as established.
4. **Evidence quality is weak across facets 2–3**: single cases (GE, NG, the Salvato patient), small groups (n=9–39), heterogeneous tasks, one dominant research group/era (1990s–2010s) for self-touch enhancement. Likely publication bias toward positive cases.
5. **Full texts I could not read** (403/paywall): Salvato 2023 *Neurocase*, White & Aimola Davies 2013, Mora 2023, Caggiano 2020, Moro 2016, Shergill 2003 (abstract + secondary descriptions only). Claims from these rest on abstracts or on van Stralen et al.'s summary; the specific parameters of Valentini et al. and White et al.'s localisation experiment are second-hand via that review and should be checked against the originals before publication.
6. **Web search was unavailable** (no search API key configured — Tavily/Brave/Exa/Firecrawl/Ollama). I worked around it by querying the Europe PMC REST API and PMC directly, which covers indexed biomedical literature well but misses theses, conference abstracts, non-indexed journals and grey literature. A configured search key would strengthen coverage, particularly for any negative or unpublished stroke force-matching work.

## Tools
- `web_search` — unavailable (no engine configured); not retried after the initial failure, per protocol.
- `web_fetch` — used against the Europe PMC REST API (`/search`, `resultType=lite` and `core`) and `pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov` for full text; several endpoints returned HTTP 403/500 (Europe PMC article pages, `fullTextXML`), handled by switching to the PMC HTML route.
- `web_fetch_pdf`, `pdf_info`, `pdf_extract`, `pdf_search` — not needed; no PDF sources were reached.
